case.summary: A two-phase product strategy to help multi-loan customers first control repayment risk, then prevent it earlier.
case.headline: Helping borrowers avoid late payments before they happen.

Two-phase product strategy for controlling and preventing repayment risk

content.body:
VPBank’s lending growth means more customers are managing multiple repayment obligations at once.
The opportunity was not simply to remind them earlier, but to help them make better decisions before repayment risk becomes urgent.
content.heading: Growth creates value — and more repayment complexity.

content.body:
The real problem was not a lack of reminders.
Customers could know each loan individually and still struggle to see the full repayment picture — especially when money became limited.
content.heading: The problem was not another repayment reminder.

content.body:
I treated the initial problem as a hypothesis and followed the repayment journey before deciding what to build.
The recurring pattern was clear: fragmented visibility led to late awareness, then weak prioritization when options were already limited.
content.heading: I treated the initial problem as a hypothesis.

content.body:
Better reminders were not enough.
A reminder can tell customers that payment is due. It cannot recover money that has already been spent.
The opportunity shifted from:

REMIND
“Your payment is due.”
to:
DECIDE
“You may be short. Here is what needs attention first.”

See the risk → Understand it → Act early
content.heading: Repayment risk starts before the due date.

content.body:
I chose decision support over more reminders, full budgeting, or heavy automation.
Start by helping customers control an existing shortfall, then move upstream to prevent that shortfall from being created.
content.heading: Control first. Prevent next.

content.body:
The solution became two connected experiences: Control → Prevent.
Phase 1 helps customers recover when repayment risk already exists; Phase 2 helps protect repayment money before spending creates that risk.
If prevention fails:
Phase 2 → Shortfall → Phase 1
content.heading: Two connected experiences: Control → Prevent

content.body:
Because these concepts have not been launched, I would validate behavior change rather than claim business impact.
The key test is whether customers change a decision early enough to reduce shortfalls and improve repayment outcomes.
content.heading: Measure behavior change, not feature usage.

content.body:
Looking back, I started too close to the repayment moment.
The more I worked through the problem, the more I realized that helping customers recover is useful — but preventing the problem earlier may be more valuable.
I would still need real customer behavior to prove whether that assumption is true.
content.heading: The product opportunity moved upstream.
